title: Elara — Chapter 1: The Duty
subtitle: The enemy princess in chains… and you hold the key.

lines: They come for you at first light. Not the dungeon — a windowless room off the guardhouse, and the moment the door opens your heart stops: bound to a post in the centre is Nessa.
Six months since you've seen her. Thinner, paler, her dress torn — but alive, and when she sees you her frightened face crumples with a relief so total it nearly puts you on your knees.
"You came," she breathes. "I knew you'd—"

"Quiet," Vance says, stepping from the corner. He lays a hand on a cane resting on the table. "The princess has a secret pain hasn't moved. So we'll give her a reason that isn't about her at all." He holds the cane out to you, handle first. "Twenty strokes. You'll deliver them. Then you'll tell the princess exactly what you've done, and beg her to make it stop."
"No," you hear yourself say. "Take me instead—"

"Hurting you accomplishes nothing," Vance says, unbothered. "But hurting *her* — that's a thing the princess will not be able to bear in *you.* Take the cane, or I hand it to a man who'll enjoy it, and we make it forty."
The same arithmetic that has owned you since the first night. Twenty strokes from your hand, as soft as you dare — or far worse from someone else's.
You take the cane, hand shaking. Nessa twists to find your face, and when she understands, she doesn't scream. She steadies.

"It's alright," she says through her tears. "I scratched the warning. I know it's not you, the same way it was never you with her. Better your hand than theirs. Do it. I can take twenty." She turns her face back to the post and sets her shoulders and waits — nineteen years old, braver than she should ever have to be.
You make the first stroke as light as you dare — still it lands, and a thin line of fire blooms across her back. "One," Vance counts.
You make yourself do the second, the third. By the fifth she's crying openly; by the eighth the cries have become small involuntary pleas — not to you, just a body begging the world to stop hurting.

Halfway through she finds your eyes again, streaming, and still tries to give you something to hold onto. "Keep going," she gasps. "I'd rather all twenty from you than one more minute of *him.* Stay with me. Count them with me."
You count with her in your head, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, each number a small private apology that will never be enough. Vance watches with the serene attention of a man confirming a theory.

At twenty you drop the cane and you're at the post before you've decided to move, catching her as she sags into your arms. Shaking, welted, but alive and conscious, and the first thing she does is grip your sleeve. "See? Twenty. Told you. We're alright."
"Touching," says Vance, retrieving his cane. "Take her back," he tells the soldiers, and the door closes on her, leaving you with the superintendent and the long walk still ahead.
"Now," Vance says, brushing off his coat. "Down to the princess. Tell her what you did, spare her no detail — I'll be asking the guards. And then beg."

"Understand the shape of this. Today was twenty strokes. Tomorrow is worse, climbing every day, until either she gives me the Everspring or the week runs out and we hang her anyway. You have six days to talk her into saving a life. I suggest you're persuasive."
The seven steps have never felt longer. Elara lifts her head at your boots, then sees your face, the blood that isn't yours, and her expression changes. "What did they do," she says. Not a question.
So you kneel and tell her. About Nessa, the post, the cane, the twenty strokes your own hand delivered. You watch each word land on her like a blow of its own.

When you've finished, Elara is silent, then very low and steady: "So that's his game. He couldn't break me with my body, so he'll break me with yours. With hers." Her eyes close. "There is no torture he could invent for my own flesh that would touch me like the thought of that girl under a cane because of my silence."
She opens her eyes, wet and fierce. "You're going to beg me now. He told you to. So beg. Get it over with."
And you can't. To truly beg her is to ask her to hand the cruelest man alive the power to never die, and some part of you better than your fear won't let your mouth form the plea.

"I can't," you whisper instead. "I've *seen* him. If a man like that never dies— but she's my sister, she's nineteen, and I don't *know* what to do. For the first time in my whole life I don't know what to do." You bow your head, and a grown man comes apart on a dungeon floor.

Elara leans forward as far as her bonds allow, her voice the gentlest thing in that black place. "You will not beg, and I will not break — not today. We are cleverer than this man, and we will not let him win by panicking on the first day of six."
"Six days," she whispers. "He's given us six days to find a third road — one that isn't my silence killing her or my secret damning the world. There's always a third road. Help me find it."
You climb the steps that night with nothing solved, and behind you in the dark, for the first time, the princess is not waiting to die. She is beginning to plan.
— End of Chapter 11 —

Day two. They came before the torches had even been changed, and not to Elara's cell — to the stripped room, a drain in the floor and a long iron trough brimmed with water so cold ice had formed at its edges. Vance was already there. Bound to a stool beside it, in the same torn shift, was Nessa.
Nineteen years old, wrists lashed behind her, lips already grey-blue from a night in this cold, eyes finding yours with a terror she tried so hard to swallow for your sake.
"Good. The brother." Vance trailed two fingers across the iced surface. "Cold leaves nothing for a magistrate to see and everything for a brother to remember."

"You're going to put her under. Not me. You. Every time I ask a question and don't like the silence, her face goes in the water, and you count to ten while she drowns a little. And when you can't bear it, you'll go tell your princess the only way to dry your sister off is to tell me where Everspring is."
"I don't know where it is. I'm a guard," you said.
"Of course you don't. You're not the one I'm asking — you're the one I'm *using.* She'll talk to keep you from this." He gestured at the trough. "Begin."
Two other men stood in the room. You understood, with sick clarity, that if you refused, they would do it instead, and would not count to ten.

So you knelt behind your sister and put your hands on her thin shoulders. "Nessa," you breathed. "Hold your breath when I press. I'll bring you up. I swear it." She nodded — one small, shaking nod — and that broke something in you that has not mended since.
"Where is Everspring?" Vance asked the empty air. Silence. "Down."
You pushed your own sister's face into the ice-water and counted while she thrashed, pulled her up gasping and alive, and Vance said it again, and you did it again.

Four times. Five. You lost count of how many times you drowned the only blood you had left and brought her back. Between them she sobbed your name — never in blame, that was unbearable — the way a child asks the one person who's supposed to make things stop to please make it stop.
"Enough for the morning," Vance said at last, bored. "Go down. Beg. Come back when she's ready to be reasonable."
They let you wrap Nessa in your own coat before dragging her back — the only mercy you could win. Then you walked down to Elara's dark, sleeves soaked, not knowing how you'd say it.
She heard the water before you spoke, as she always did. "You're wet," she said quietly. "What did they make you do."

And you told her — the trough, the ice, your own hands, Nessa saying your name. She could only take it through your voice, which is its own cruelty. You felt her go very still in her chains as you spoke.

"He's not torturing her," she said at last, low and terrible with understanding. "He's torturing *you.* Through her, through me — instruments he's playing to find the note that makes me open my mouth. He's very good. So we stop fighting like this. Starting now, we do the one thing he isn't watching for."
"What thing," you said.
"We start *looking.* Six days — he keeps saying it to break us. I'm going to use it. Every time he sends you down here to break, you're going to bring me the room instead."

"When you walk these halls, you're a broken man begging — let him believe it. But while you beg, you *count.* Guards on the stair at the change of watch. When the torches are renewed and who carries the keys. Where the cold air comes from — a way out, always. The rope on the upper beam, the drain in that stripped room, the door they never quite bolt."

"Don't plan anything yet. Just bring me the room, piece by piece, until I can walk it in the dark. Count the guards at the night change. Bring me that tomorrow. We have six days, and I am done spending them on grief."

You climbed the stair that night with your sleeves still damp — but for the first time, counting. Two guards at the lower landing, one at the upper, a torch-bearer at the third watch with keys on his left hip.
Small things. Nothing things. The beginning of everything. Day two of six was over — four more, and a soldier who had finally, quietly, decided to win.
— End of Chapter 12 —

The days after the trough blurred into one grey ache. Vance's lever — the cane, the cold, the begging cycle — went on not working. On the fourth day the king lost patience with the whole design: word came down that Nessa was moved off the table, back to an ordinary cell, fed, untouched.

It also meant the leash on your throat had gone slack. Those blurred nights, you brought Elara the room, piece by piece — watch-change, keys, the cold draft from a bricked-over drain — until the escape was nearly ready.
Then they told you the execution was set for dawn — and tonight, the king himself was coming down to ask her one last time.

King Mordane came without fanfare — a tall, unhurried man in plain wool, a mage at his shoulder, four soldiers carrying something heavy under a cloth. He looked like a tired clerk. That was the most frightening thing about him.
"So this is her," he said, studying Elara in her chains. "Smaller than the stories." His eyes moved to you. "And this is the one who's grown fond of her. Stay. I want a witness who'll feel it."
The soldiers pulled the cloth away — a curved frame of black iron, its arc rising to a cruel apex. A cradle, if a cradle were made to break the thing it held.

"Strip the blindfold," the king said. "I want her to watch her own king be reasonable." And to you: "Help them lay her over it. I'm told you have gentle hands. Use them. It will be the last gentleness she gets from anyone."

They forced you to lay the small of her back against the iron apex, wrists to one side, ankles to the other, until her whole body bent backward over the curve. She made no sound — only found your eyes and held them: not your fault, we are not done.

Then the soldiers hung weights from her cuffs, and the arch deepened, and the half-healed lash-scars along her breast split open, fresh blood running into the iron. She gasped, the first sound, through her teeth.

The king crouched, and produced a small clay jar. "Salt and vinegar," he said, holding it out to you. "You have the gentlest hands, so it should be yours. Refuse, and the mage does it, and you're flogged beside her. Choose quickly."

So your hands poured salt and vinegar into the torn lines along her breast, and the scream that tore out of her filled the dungeon. She knew it was you, and still did not blame you. "Where is the Everspring, Elara?" the king asked over her screaming, in the tone one uses to ask the hour.

She wept and shook on the iron, and when she could make words, they weren't the ones he wanted. "You'll get nothing from me, clerk-king. The spring dies with me. A man who wants to live forever must *never* be allowed to."
Something flickered in Mordane's tired face — not anger. Almost respect. It was worse than anger.

The king didn't rage. He nodded, as if she'd confirmed something, and pressed the jar back into your hands. "Again, deeper. And hear my offer, Princess — I make it once. One word and there's no gallows at dawn. A quiet room, a window, your sister Liora safe forever. Speak, and you both walk out breathing."
"Pour," he told you softly. "Let her think it over with the salt in her."

So you poured again, and she screamed again, her arched body wrenching against the chains — and again, and again. "Where is the Everspring?" Touch. Scream. "Liora, safe. A life." Touch. Scream. He never raised his voice, certain that everyone breaks if you're calm enough about it.

You stood there pouring agony into the woman you loved because the alternative was the mage's crueler hands and the frame beside her. And she would not break — not for the salt, not for the offer of a life, not for Liora's name in the king's mouth. Bent backward, breast laid open, she would not give him the spring.
The king straightened. "More weight. The big stones. Hang them on the wrists and ankles both — I want her spine to learn what it's arguing with."

You and a soldier hung the quarry-stones from her cuffs, and with each one the arch deepened further than a body is built to go, her spine standing up under the stretched skin. She made a sound with each one you will hear for the rest of your life.
With four stones hung, the king laid his open hand on her straining belly. "You're a finger's breadth from never standing again, Princess. One more stone, or four words — *it is at* — and the name."

"One," he said. "Two." And at *three* — when you stood frozen with the fifth stone in your arms — she dragged in a breath and said, in a thread of a voice: "Burn... first." Something in his patience finally thinned.

He stood, and set the sole of his boot against her bared throat — slow, measured, easing down onto her windpipe while she lay pinned and could not turn her head. Her face went dark; you lunged half a step before a spear-haft caught you across the chest.

At the very edge, he lifted his boot, let her claw back one lungful, and asked gently: "Where is the Everspring?" She did not speak. Three times he took her to the edge of the dark and three times she gave him her silence instead of her air.

The king stopped first, not for mercy. He took the empty jar from your hands and looked at her with something like wonder. "Eleven years I've hunted that water, and the last door is a girl who'd rather burn than open."
"But I am patient, and I have one night left. Leave her on it, exactly as she is — the stones stay, the bend stays. And I won't have her sleeping through it. Rig the basin."

They hung a copper basin pricked with pinholes above her and made you haul it up dripping — cold water falling on her upturned face and raw wounds all night, just often enough that she could never fall away into sleep.

"By dawn," the king said, watching the first drops fall, "either she gives me the spring or she gives the city a quiet hanging. Both serve." At the stair he paused, almost to himself: "A pity. She was the only honest thing in this whole castle."

Then he was gone. "You've served your purpose, gentle hands," Vance said, steering you toward the steps while two fresh guards took the watch. "You'll have her back at dawn, what's left of her, for the walk to the rope."

You climbed the long stair with the drip of the basin following you into the dark — a half-cut key and a sleeping-draught in your boot, and no way past two fresh guards to reach her. Dawn was the execution. You did not sleep either.
— End of Chapter 13 —

Dawn came grey and certain. They lifted her off the cradle — three days without sleep and a night bent backward had left her barely able to stand; her spine would not unbend all at once, tearing a sound out of her with each stage. They half-carried her out into light she hadn't seen in weeks.
The whole city had come, packing the square shoulder to shoulder, and when she appeared, blinking and broken, the sound they made was not human — a wall of hate with ten thousand throats.

They stood her on the scaffold beneath the rope. King Mordane raised one hand and the square fell silent. "People of the capital, this woman has been asked for one thing that would buy her life. I'll ask her once more, where you can all hear it." He turned to her. "The Everspring, Elara. Speak, and you live. Stay silent, and these good people watch you drop."

She lifted her head, and let the whole square see her ruined face. "Your king wants to live forever. That is the secret he's tortured me three weeks to buy. Not safety — *forever.* Ask yourselves what a man like this does with a thousand years." She swayed, caught herself. "I will die today so that he cannot. It is the best gift I will ever give your children. Pull the rope."

It was the wrong thing for the king. A murmur went through the crowd — a flicker of unease, a question planted in ten thousand heads: *forever?* He could not afford to let the rope make a martyr of her with that word hanging in the air.
"No," he said, lowering his hand. "A quick drop is too clean for what she's earned. Today she answers to *you.*"
They locked her into a pillory at the scaffold's edge — a heavy oak frame clamping neck and wrists, bending her forward stooped and helpless.

"Three weeks my questioners had her, and got nothing," the king called. "Perhaps the people she wronged will do better. She stands here until dusk. Only she does not die — she is mine to hang, when I choose."
He set you and a line of guards around the foot of the pillory — not to protect her, to protect his property. Your orders: keep the mob from killing her, and let them do everything short of it.
So you stood between the woman you loved and the city that wanted her dead, your sword permitted only to keep her alive for a worse death.

They came in a flood — rotten fruit, filth, spit — a whole city emptying its hate onto a woman who could not raise a hand to wipe her own eyes. An old man struck her across the face with a switch until a guard shoved him back.

Some of them had earned this — the woman weeping while she threw, the man saying a son's name with every stone. Elara had burned their fields. The grief in that square was real, and there was no clean place to stand in it.

By midday a woman climbed up with shears and hacked off her hair to a roar; it fell into the muck and was trampled. A thrown cobble opened her brow and blood ran into her eyes she couldn't wipe — and still, every hour, she lifted her clamped head as far as the oak allowed and faced them, and would not weep for them, and would not beg.

Twice, men threw stones meant to kill. Both times you moved without deciding to — your shield took one, you knocked the other's arm aside. She felt it. Once, when you were near enough, she breathed two words through her split lips, just for you: "Not yet." Telling you to hold — not to throw it all away saving her in front of ten thousand witnesses.
It went on until the light went amber and the crowd's arm finally tired. By dusk the square was emptying, and what was left in the pillory barely moved.

Vance came to unlock her. "Still breathing," he noted, tilting her ruined face by the chin. "The king hasn't set a new day for the rope. You'll hang when you break, and not before. Could be tomorrow. Could be a long, long time."

They carried her down into the dark, and you were the one who washed the filth and blood from her, hands shaking. Neither of you said what you both now knew: there was no execution date left to escape *before* — only an open stretch of days in which the king would hurt her until she died of it, on no schedule but his patience.
The clock you'd been racing was gone. And a man with no deadline stops waiting for the perfect night, and starts making one.

She slept at last that night, the dead sleep of a body with nothing left, her bare head in your lap, your back to the cell door — while you sat awake counting guards, watch-changes, the cold breath of the bricked drain, turning the half-cut key over in your fingers.
No deadline. No perfect night. Just a princess who had told a whole city the truth and lived, and a guard who had finally, fully run out of reasons to wait.
— End of Chapter 14 —

The king had no calendar now, and that made him worse. For days he let her rot, then found a new road: your sister. "Pain behind a door is a rumor," he said. "Pain in the sun is a lever. We'll do it where the city can watch her choose."

They built it in the open ground below the walls: a timber A-frame, a pulley-wheel at its peak, one rope with a noosed cuff at each end. A crowd was already gathering — the same city that had stoned her.
They made *you* rig it. Vance stood over you while you tied your sister's wrists, then the princess's, and threaded the rope, learning knot by knot exactly how the cruelty worked.

Vance walked the crowd through it like a showman. "Simple, and fair. The girl on this side is weak. The princess is strong, so we let the strong one carry the weak one. We hang weights on Her Highness — as long as she holds them, the girl stands easy. The moment the princess sags, the girl is hauled up off the earth by her bound arms until her shoulders leave their sockets. The princess decides, with her own strength, whether the child is hurt."

Then they loaded her — bar after bar of iron on her wrist-cuffs, drawing her arms up and back until even she made a low animal sound. Within minutes the skin of her shoulders went a deep, furious red, the blood trapped and pounding where the cords bit.

Nessa, too weak to hold herself steady, kept giving; every time she faltered the pull hauled the princess up onto her toes, shoulders screaming, until she fought her heels back down and steadied them both.

"Hold still, Nessa," Elara breathed across the gap. "Don't fight it, sweetheart. I have you. Stand, and let me hold us both." Your sister wept and tried, and every failure the princess paid for in her arms — and never once let the rope drop her.
The king watched, unsatisfied — holding is not breaking. "Vance. Give her a reason to fall, and let's see if she'll let the girl drop to spare her own skin. Whip her."

Something lit in Vance's face worse than cruelty — gratitude. Here was his road back into favor, and it ran across the princess's body. "You've cost me a great deal, Highness," he said quietly. "Let me return some of it."

The first lash fell across her breast, over the half-healed scars, laying them bare again. But the true cruelty was what it demanded: if she flinched and her arms dropped even a hand's breadth, Nessa would be torn off the earth. So she could not flinch — had to take each stroke standing dead still, absorbing the whip into a body forbidden to move.

Vance laid the whip across her front again and again, and each one she met without falling. Between the lashes she didn't curse him or beg the king — she spoke to your sister. "Almost done, Nessa. Watch your brother in the line — he's going to get you home. Just stand, love."
You stood in the guard-line where she'd told the girl to look, watching the bravest thing you'd ever see, knowing you'd tied the knots that made it possible.

Once, Nessa's legs went entirely, and the rope snatched Elara up entirely off the ground, screaming at last — then she got a toe down, dragged it back, and gasped, "It's all right. I've got you. Stand." She would have died on that rope before dropping the girl. Everyone could see it, even the king.

It was Vance's arm that tired first. He had whipped her past any count, and she had not fallen, had not given the spring, had not let Nessa touch the air — a torturer who cannot break his victim has proven her unbreakable in front of everyone watching.
The king rose and ended it, not from mercy. "Enough. Take them down." Under his breath: "...she should have broken. Why won't she break."

They lowered the iron. Nessa, whole, saved by a woman whipped raw rather than drop her an inch, collapsed into your arms; Elara folded into the dirt, arms hanging wrong, conscious only enough to see the girl was whole.
"Told you," she whispered. "I had her."

That night you sat between them in the dark, and something in you finished changing. There was no deadline to beat, no perfect night coming — only a woman who would let herself be destroyed before his cruelty won.
You did not turn the half-cut key over in your fingers that night. You finished cutting it.
— End of Chapter 15 —

It took two days to be ready — cutting, filing, stealing what the run would need: a coil of rope, a skiff hidden in the reeds below the river outflow, dry clothes, the blue vial that had ridden in your boot since the day you made it.

On the third night, the castle gave you your window: a feast for Vance in the great hall, the garrison drinking his health till the torches guttered, and a storm walking up the river, swelling the black water, drowning the night in noise. Everything you'd waited for came at once. You stopped waiting.

You carried the dungeon-watch their wine yourself, the blue vial thumbed empty into the jug. Within the quarter-hour both men on the lower landing were snoring. The third-watch torch-bearer came round at his hour, and when he folded you eased him down and lifted the key-ring from his belt. Two doors' worth of iron. Nessa, and Elara.

You went down to her first — some compass in you pointed there and would not be argued with. The deepest cell was black and close, full of the storm's sound through the stone and her shallow, careful breathing. Your hand shook so badly the key chattered against the lock before it turned, and the door you had locked a hundred times swung open for you for the first time.
She heard the wrong sound and flinched back into the straw, bracing for whatever new thing they'd built. "...Whatever it is," she whispered, "do it and let me sleep. I'll still say no—"

"Elara." You were on your knees before you knew you'd moved. "It's me. Listen — the watch is down, the storm's covering us, the feast has the rest of them drunk, and there's a boat in the reeds below the river drain. Do you understand what I'm telling you?"
She went very still, then came awake all at once. "Say it again," she breathed. "Plainly, so I know it's you and not my own mind being cruel."
"Tonight," you said, taking her cold face in both hands. "Tonight I take you out of here. Both of you. There's only us, and a hole in the wall, and a river. I'm taking you home."

She made a sound that was not a sob and not a laugh and somehow both, and pressed her wet face into your palm — the same hand that had loosened her cords the first night and poured salt into her wounds on the worst one. That she'd still turn toward it undid you completely.
"All right," she whispered against your skin. "I believe you. Get these off me and take me out of the dark."

You found the cuffs by touch — her wrists raw and crusted from the weights — and worked the iron loose as gently as your shaking hands allowed. When the last fell away, her arms dropped uselessly, shoulders wrenched too far to lift. She gave a small broken laugh. "They don't work. You'll have to carry me out like luggage."
"Then I'll carry you," you said. "Let me be the strong one for one night."

She leaned her forehead against yours, the only part of her that still obeyed her, and stayed there breathing you in. "Do you know," she murmured, "you are the only gentle thing that has happened to me since the snow. They sent me a guard to keep me alive so they could destroy me, and instead he's the reason there was anything left worth destroying. I held on for a thousand reasons. The last one was you."

And then — a storm above, a boat below, a whole life of waited-for things pressing on this one moment — you closed the last inch of dark between you and kissed her. Gently, mindful of her split lip, a kiss that asked nothing and promised everything. She couldn't raise her arms, so she gave the only thing her body would still surrender — kissing you back, fierce and trembling and alive, while the rain came down.

When you parted she was crying and smiling at once, and so were you. "That was a very stupid thing to do with the watch only drugged. Do it once more anyway." So you did — then made yourself stop, because love wouldn't get her over the wall and time would. You slid your arms beneath her and lifted her out of the straw she'd bled into for a month.
She weighed almost nothing — its own grief, how much of her they'd taken — but settled against your chest as if made to fit there, and let out a long shuddering breath.
"I have you," you said into her hair — her own words to your sister, given back to her now. "The dark doesn't. Not anymore."

"I hear you," she whispered. "Then go. Get your sister, and get us all to that river." Quieter still: "...I'm not finished with you, guardsman. When we're free, we're going to have a very long conversation about the rest of our lives."

You carried her into the black throat of the dungeon stair, her heartbeat against your ribs, the storm roaring above, the drugged watch sprawled behind you and the whole sleeping castle between you and the river.

Two doors of iron warm in your pocket. A sister waiting one floor up. It was not over — Vance was still drinking his own health one hall away — but for the length of that first staircase, with her against your heart, you let yourself believe it could be done.
— End of Chapter 16 —
The upper cells were drier, the torches farther apart, the cold coming from the river now — swollen and furious beyond the wall, the storm feeding it.

You set Elara down in the deepest shadow at the stair-turn. "Nessa is up there," you breathed. "Last cell, end of the gallery, and a guard. I need you to stay here — you can barely stand." She gripped your sleeve with the hand that still worked.

"I have spent two years learning to be useful in chains," she whispered. "Do not make me start being useless the night I'm out of them. You'll need both hands for your sister. Let me be the thing the guard is looking at instead."
You hated that she was right. "If it goes wrong," you said, "you scream the wall down and run for the drain. Don't come back for me."
"Liar," she said gently. "You'd never obey that order either." And she let go of your sleeve.

The gallery guard, Holt, was bored, his back to the cells, face to a slit window watching the rain. Elara went first — walking, not creeping, the way only the highborn can even barefoot and ruined. She let her shackle-chain drag once so it sang. Holt turned, hand on his cudgel, and forgot the cudgel entirely.

"You are the new watch?" she said, her voice low and warm, a voice from a banquet, not a cell. "They send a man like you to guard empty rooms. What a waste." She came closer than a prisoner should dare. "Tell me your name, watchman. I would like one kind face to remember from this place."

It shouldn't have worked — Holt had been told she was a viper — but she turned the full charm of a court on a lonely man on a long night, and he stepped toward her, turned fully away from the cells, and started to say his name.
Behind him, you came up the gallery on bare feet, the key-ring strangled in your fist so it couldn't ring.

Nessa's cell was the last. Through the bars, nineteen and grey-faced, awake, her wrists in a short wall-chain. She jerked toward the bars; you put one finger to your lips so hard it hurt. She went still and silent, only her eyes screaming. The lock took the second key and opened like a held breath let go.

The wrist-chain was the problem — riveted to a ring sunk in the wall, no key would touch it. You wedged the chisel where the ring met the stone, packing your cloak around it to swallow the sound. The mortar came away slowly, in wet grey crumbs, every scrape a noise in a quiet castle.
Down the gallery, Holt laughed at something the princess said. Good. Laughter is loud.

Elara kept him — the murmur, the low laugh, walking him in a slow half-circle until his back was to the whole gallery. Once she laughed bright and delighted at nothing, exactly when your chisel shrieked on stone.

The mortar gave. The ring tore loose with a gout of grit, and Nessa's chain dropped slack into your hands. You pulled her up — she weighed nothing — and she pressed her face into your neck and shook, silent, and you held her the way you had when she was small.

"Sister," you breathed. "I have you. We're going. Not a sound." She nodded, then lifted her head to look past you at the woman still holding a guard in the palm of her voice. Recognition crossed her face. "That's her," she mouthed. "That's the one you talk to in your sleep."

You bundled Nessa's chain up short and started back down the gallery. Now the only trouble left was Holt — and a man cannot stare at a princess forever, not with his relief due and some animal part of him wondering why the empty cells smell of fresh-broken mortar.

Elara felt it turning before you did. "Walk me to the window," she told Holt, gaily, stepping to put her body between his eyes and the three of you slipping behind him toward the stair. "I want to see the storm before they hang me." Holt, helpless, walked her to the window, and the gallery emptied of everyone he was charged to keep.

You reached the stairhead with Nessa pressed to your back. Elara let the guard have one last moment, then simply drifted away from him into the dark, your hand finding her wrist and drawing her down the steps. Holt blinked at the empty window a long while before understanding the most beautiful thing that had ever happened to him had been a thief.

Three of you now on the cold lower stair — a broken princess, a starved sister, a guard who'd betrayed everything he was sworn to. Nessa's hand in your left, Elara's in your right, both finally on the same side of the wall.
"The drain," Elara whispered. "Take us to the wall that breathes."

You went down toward the river-sound and the staged skiff. Behind you the castle slept on, not yet knowing its cruelest cell was empty and the princess it meant to hang was walking out through its own foundations. It would know soon. But not yet.
— End of Chapter 17 —

You took them down through the foundations the way you had walked it a hundred times in your head — the cold lower passage where the drain breathed, the loosened stones you had worked over a dozen night-watches, the dark that smelled of river instead of iron.

Elara could not climb and Nessa could barely walk, so you went slow, a hand on each of them. You were perhaps thirty paces from the breathing stones when, far above and behind you, the castle stopped sleeping.
It began as one bell. Then every bell.

Vance had not gone to bed. A captain restored to favor does not sleep on the night of his triumph — and somewhere between the feast and his quarters he had gone down to look at the woman who had cost him everything and given it back.
He found the lower landing strewn with snoring men, a cell standing open and empty, chains lying cut on the straw, still warm, and the second key gone from the torch-bearer's ring.

Vance was many cruel things but never a fool. He understood the whole of it in a single breath — the guard, the looks, the weak draught, the princess who would not break — and he threw back his head and roared the castle awake.

The order went out in his voice, carrying down the stairwells like cold water: "The traitor has the enemy princess and his own sister! Every gate, every wall! Gold to whoever brings her back breathing — and the guard's head I want myself!"

Hundreds of boots, all at once, in every corridor of the keep. You reached the breathing stones and put your shoulder to the mortar you had patiently murdered over a month of stolen nights. The old, forgotten sally-port gave way into a gust of wet wind and the open, storm-black night.

You poured all three of you out onto the slick rock above the river. The staged skiff waited in the reeds, pale in the dark — not forty paces downstream. Forty paces between you and the black water that would carry you free.
You never got to take them.

Torches spilled out of the broken wall behind you — and more came around the foot of the tower ahead, a line of them fanning across the rock. Vance had not only chased; he had sent men around the outside. In a dozen heartbeats you went from almost-free to surrounded: the three of you backed against the roaring river, soldiers closing from both sides.

You drew the short guard's blade at your hip — one sword, against a tightening ring of spears, a wounded princess at your back and your sister clinging to your arm. It was not a fight. It was the few seconds before an ending.
And then Elara stepped past you.

She stepped past you into the torchlight and the rain — and it struck you like a blow that it was the first time in two years you had seen her stand with nothing on her wrists. No chains. No shackles. No rope. Just a princess on her own two feet under an open sky.

She did not reach for your sword. She did not reach for a fallen spear. She let her empty hands hang loose at her sides, and slowly, deliberately, she rolled the wreck of her shoulders back and lifted her chin, and you realized you were about to see something the king's dungeon had never once let out of her.

"Save your sister." She did not look back at you; her eyes were already moving over the soldiers, counting, measuring. "That is the only order I have ever given you that I need you to obey. Get Nessa to the high country. I will hold them here."
"Elara—" Your voice broke on it.

"Before I was a prisoner, before I was ever a princess of war," she said, very quietly, "I was a child in the training courts of my mother's house, and they taught me the open-hand forms before they ever let me hold a blade. Two years of iron did not take that out of me. Let these men learn what my homeland teaches its daughters."

She bent for one quick moment and tore the trailing, sodden hem of her ruined skirt, knotting the wet fabric short and tight against her thigh so it could not foul her legs — a fighter clearing her own footwork, nothing more. Then she set her bare feet on the wet stone, sank her weight low, and drew her hands up before her in a guard you had never seen: one palm open and forward, one drawn back at the hip, elbows soft, breathing slow.

From somewhere far inside her, under the brand and the lash-scars and the wrenched shoulders, an old voice surfaced — her first master's, from a sunlit courtyard a lifetime and a war away. Stillness first, the voice said. Let them bring you the fight. You do not have to be stronger than ten men. You have to be exactly where they are not.
She breathed out. She waited.

The first soldier came fast and clumsy, spear leveled at her belly. She did not back away from it — she stepped in, off the line, turning her hips, and let his own lunge carry him past her; her forward palm snapped up under his jaw with the whole turn of her body behind it, and his head went back and his feet went out and he hit the rock and did not rise.
One, she thought. The form is still in me. Thank the old gods, it is still in me.

Her split lip was bleeding again and she had not even felt the strike land. It was almost peaceful. For the first time in two years her body was hers, doing the thing it had been shaped to do before the world ever taught it pain.

The second and third came together, wiser, spreading to take her from two sides. She flowed between them like water finding the low ground — a low sweeping kick that took the left man's knee out from under him, a pivot, an elbow turned into the right man's ribs, a twist of his own wrist that sent his spear clattering into the dark. Down. Down.

But it cost her, and you saw it cost her. When she snapped that kick high, the strappado-wrenched shoulders screamed and her arm dropped a fraction too slow; when she twisted, the half-healed lash-wounds across her breast split open afresh under the rain, and a thin dark line bled through the ruined cloth. The torn skirt came loose mid-pivot and tangled her ankle — she ripped it free with a snarl without ever breaking the form.
Each strike was a debt her starved, tortured body could not really pay. She paid it anyway, and smiled through it, because every soldier on the ground was one more second of your sister's life.

"RUN!" she screamed — not turning, her voice cracking clean in half on the word, tears and rain streaming down a face that was still, impossibly, fighting. "For the love of everything that is left — TAKE HER AND RUN!"

Every part of you that had loosened her cords and wiped her tears and carried her up that long dark stair was screaming to stay and die at her side. You did not take a step back. You took a step toward her.
"I'm not leaving you," you said, and you barely knew you'd said it. "I came down into this place to get you out. I am not walking out of it without you—"
And then Nessa — small, starved, terrified Nessa — seized your sword-arm with both her hands and hauled you backward with all the weight she had left in her body.
"She's GIVING us this!" your sister sobbed against your shoulder. "Don't you dare waste it. Don't you dare make her do this for nothing — RUN, brother, run, RUN!"

So you turned away. It was the hardest thing you have ever done, and you will carry it the rest of your life: you turned your back on the princess fighting alone in the rain, and you ran, your sister's hand crushed in yours, up the dark track toward the high country.

Behind you the torchlight thickened. A fresh wave of soldiers was pouring out of the broken wall now, more and more of them flooding onto the narrow shelf of rock, and through the rain your last backward glimpse was of a single small figure at the center of it all — still standing, still moving, still turning men away with nothing but her hands and her feet and her unbreakable, unbroken will.
Then the track bent, and the rocks rose between you, and she was gone from your sight — but not, you swore into the storm, gone for good.
— End of Chapter 18 —

You ran until the river was a silver thread far below and the castle a distant clutch of torches, until your lungs were fire and your sister's legs were failing. You ran until the land tilted up hard and the black mountains rose enormous ahead, and only when Nessa could not take another step did you stop, on a high cold shoulder of stone, and turn, and look back the way you had come.
Far, far below, on that little shelf of rock above the water, you could still see her. And your heart stopped.
She was not holding three soldiers now. She was holding ten.

A single figure ringed in torchlight, with the black river at her back and ten armed men in a closing arc before her — and still she fought them bare-handed, the way her mother's house had taught her in a courtyard a war and a lifetime away.

Even at that terrible distance you could read the forms: the way she never met a spear straight but turned it, slid past it, used the man's own weight against him; the way she struck once, hard, exactly where he was open, and was already moving before he fell. A palm to a throat. A heel to the back of a knee. A turn that sent two of them stumbling into each other in the dark.
Hold your center, the old voice said inside her, calm as a sunlit morning. Ten men cannot all reach you at once. Make them take turns. Make each one pay.
You did not know — you could not have known — what it was costing her to make it look like that.

Inside the body that moved so beautifully, everything was failing at once. Her starved muscles burned through the last of what little they had left. The brand below her collarbone was a coal under her skin. The lash-wounds across her breast had torn fully open and the rain ran pink down the front of her ruined dress. Her wrenched shoulders shrieked with every block. And her bare feet and shins, cut to ribbons on the wet rock, left dark prints with every step she took.
One more, she told herself, each time another man came in. One breath. One form. One more, and they are one breath farther from the mountain. Hold. Just hold.

The torn skirt fought her as hard as the soldiers did. The wet, ragged cloth wound around her knees, snatched at her kicks, threatened her balance every time she pivoted, and twice she had to tear it free one-handed in the middle of the fight, snarling, refusing to let a scrap of cloth do what ten men could not.

She did not let it. She knotted it tighter, set her bleeding feet wider, and kept her center low, and went on — because somewhere on a dark mountain two people she had decided to save were still climbing, and a princess of her blood does not stop while there is one more breath of distance left to buy.
This is what I am for, she thought, almost wondering at it through the haze of pain. Not the spring. Not the throne. This. Standing between the ones I love and the dark. Let it be this.
And then, at last, it left her.

It was not one blow that did it. It was two years come due all at once — the cradle, the press, the brand, the strappado, the days without food or water or sleep — and a body, however brave, however trained, however royal, can only be spent so far before there is simply nothing left to draw on.

Her legs, cut and bleeding and shaking, finally would not answer her. A high block came a heartbeat too slow. A pivot did not turn. The beautiful, flowing forms stuttered and broke, and for the first time the ring of men was faster than she was.
A guard caught her from behind, both her wrists locked in his fists.

Even then — even spent, even finished — she did not simply give up. She dropped her weight, turned inside his grip the way the forms had taught her, tore one hand free and drove her elbow back into him so hard he folded and let go.
But it was the last of her. There was nothing after it. And the others saw it too.

Four of them closed on her at once. Then five. They caught her arms, her shoulders, bore her down by sheer weight of bodies, pinning the warrior under a press of armored men who would not have dared come within reach of her a minute before.

And still — God, still — she fought them. Weakened, swaying, half-blind with exhaustion and pain, she strained against their hands, twisting, refusing to go still, because going still was a thing she did not know how to do.
From your mountain you watched it and you could not breathe. Nessa pressed her face into your side so she would not have to see.

She knew. Some clear, calm part of her, even now, knew exactly how this ended — a whole army against one starved, chained-and-unchained princess on a strip of wet rock, and only one way for the arithmetic to come out. There was no winning this. There never had been.

She fought anyway. With every scrap of spirit left in her, with the last forms her body could still remember, she fought as though she did not know the ending at all — because the fight was never about winning. It was about the seconds, and every second was a step you and Nessa climbed farther into the dark mountains and out of their reach.

And then, between one breath and the next, the darkness simply rose up and swallowed her sight. Her body — a princess's body, born to strength, raised to it, made for it — had nothing left to give; the months of the cradle and the press and the brand and the starving had finally spent the very last of her. Her knees buckled. The torchlight smeared and went out. She folded down onto the wet stone, unconscious before she landed.

It was done, from her side. She had held them long enough. The two people she loved were safe, far up a black mountain where no soldier would follow tonight — and in the last flickering instant before everything went dark, knowing that, she smiled. And then she fainted.
Then, through the thinning rain, you saw him come.
Vance. Unhurried now. Walking out into the torchlight with chains gathered in his two hands, taking his time, savoring it — the one prize the whole night had failed to deny him.

They held her limp, senseless body still while he shackled her. Wrists first. Then the iron collar. Then the long, heavy chain — locking back onto her, link by link, every single iron thing she had stood up under the open sky to be free of, fastened now onto a woman too far gone to even feel it close.
There was no walking her back. She was long past that.

Two soldiers took her under the arms and dragged her limp between them, her cut bare feet trailing over the wet rock, her shorn head hanging loose. The princess who had held ten armed men at bay an hour before was carried off senseless, back toward the gate, back into the castle she had bled and fought and spent the very last of herself to escape.
The dark she had begged you never to let take her was taking her back, and there was not one thing on this earth you could do about it from a mountain a thousand feet above.
You stood on that high shoulder of stone and watched them carry the unconscious shape of her down off the rock, and you could not breathe, and you could not move, and you could not look away.

You will see it behind your eyes every night for the rest of your life: her head hanging, her arms loose, the chains swinging at her wrists, the torchlight swallowing her, the dark closing over her again.

Beside you, Nessa pressed her face into your side and wept, and you held her, and neither of you said a word, because there were no words left in the world for what you had just watched her do for you.
But you held on to one thing in that moment, and you will hold on to it for the rest of your days.

The last thing she did, up there in the thick of ten men, before the darkness rose and took her — you were far too distant to have truly seen it, and you knew it anyway, the way you always somehow knew her: she had smiled.

She had spent every last drop of herself and she had won the only victory she had ever wanted — yours — and knowing the two of you stood free and uncaught on a far black mountain, she had let go and gone down into the dark glad. It was the face of a woman who had lost everything and regretted nothing.
Then they hauled her through the gate, and the dark of the castle closed over the princess once more, and she did not stir.
You stood on the cold mountain with your sister's hand crushed in yours and the grey morning coming up behind you — free, and ruined, and certain of exactly one thing.
"I'm coming back for you," you said into the wind that could not carry it to her. "Whatever it takes. However long. I am coming back. I promise you — this is not how it ends for now."
— To be continued… —
